digest.headline: DeepMind dévoile Genie 4, une avancée majeure en simulation générative de mondes réalistes pour la robotique et les jeux vidéo
digest.overview: La veille du 2026-10-28 met en lumière des progrès significatifs en modélisation générative, en agents multimodaux et en optimisation des architectures. Les travaux explorent des compromis fondamentaux entre structure, efficacité et généralisation, tout en proposant des benchmarks rigoureux pour évaluer les systèmes émergents.

highlights.title: Genie 4 : simulation de mondes en temps réel
highlights.text: DeepMind présente Genie 4, un modèle capable de générer des environnements dynamiques et réalistes en temps réel. Cette innovation renforce les applications en robotique et en jeux vidéo, où la fidélité des simulations est critique. Le modèle s'appuie sur des architectures génératives avancées pour améliorer la cohérence physique et visuelle des scènes.

highlights.title: Représentations visuelles discrètes et efficacité sémantique
highlights.text: Une étude remet en cause l'idée que les tokens discrets perdent nécessairement du sens en vision. Elle montre que l'efficacité dépend du budget de bits et propose FVQ, une méthode atteignant des performances comparables aux représentations continues. Cela ouvre des pistes pour optimiser les modèles multimodaux sans sacrifier la précision.

highlights.title: Agents multimodaux et dynamique physique
highlights.text: PDRVLA et ThinkWorld introduisent des modules de dynamique physique pour les modèles Vision-Language-Action (VLA), améliorant la génération d'actions robotiques. PDRVLA évite la latence liée à la prédiction vidéo, tandis que ThinkWorld combine raisonnement en chaîne de dynamique et apprentissage par renforcement. Ces approches démontrent des taux de succès élevés sur plusieurs benchmarks.

highlights.title: Benchmarks pour agents proactifs et induction d'habitudes
highlights.text: Omni-InteractScope et HABIT-Bench évaluent respectivement les capacités d'interaction proactive dans des flux audiovisuels continus et l'induction d'habitudes à partir de données faibles. Les résultats révèlent des limites critiques, notamment dans l'invocation d'outils et la généralisation des habitudes, soulignant des défis persistants pour les agents autonomes.

highlights.title: Optimisation et sécurité des LLM
highlights.text: Des travaux comme *Follow the Gradient* et *SimpleLoRIF* proposent des méthodes pour identifier et filtrer les données de fine-tuning dégradant la sécurité des LLM. Par ailleurs, *Multiscale Policy Optimization* améliore l'optimisation des agents LLM à long terme en allouant des crédits à l'échelle des tours, réduisant ainsi les coûts computationnels.

highlights.title: Écart structurel et raisonnement formel
highlights.text: Une démonstration théorique et empirique montre que les modèles sans connaissance explicite de la structure d'un problème nécessitent des données infinies pour égaler les performances d'un modèle structuré. En parallèle, *h1* prouve qu'un agent simple avec réflexion autonome peut rivaliser avec des workflows spécialisés en preuve formelle, questionnant la complexité des architectures dédiées.

digest.trend: Les avancées récentes confirment une tendance vers l'intégration de dynamiques physiques et de mécanismes de mémoire structurée dans les agents multimodaux, tout en soulignant l'importance des benchmarks rigoureux pour évaluer leur généralisation. Parallèlement, l'optimisation des architectures et des coûts computationnels reste un enjeu central, avec des compromis de plus en plus fins entre performance et efficacité.

items.title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
items.tldr: Genie 4 de DeepMind est un modèle de simulation du monde en temps réel, améliorant le réalisme des environnements générés. Innovation majeure en modélisation générative, avec des implications pour la robotique et les jeux vidéo.

deep_analysis.probleme: Genie 4 vise à résoudre le défi de la simulation réaliste et interactive d'environnements virtuels en temps réel. Il cherche à combler le fossé entre les mondes simulés statiques ou préprogrammés et des simulations dynamiques capables de réagir de manière cohérente et crédible aux actions des utilisateurs ou des agents, tout en maintenant un haut niveau de fidélité visuelle et physique.
deep_analysis.methode: Genie 4 s'appuie sur une architecture de modèle génératif avancé, combinant des techniques de deep learning, notamment des réseaux de neurones transformers et des modèles de diffusion, pour prédire et générer des états futurs d'un environnement simulé. Le système utilise des données massives issues de vidéos et d'interactions réelles pour entraîner un modèle capable de comprendre et de reproduire les lois physiques et les dynamiques complexes des mondes virtuels. Une attention particulière est portée à l'intégration de mécanismes de rétroaction en temps réel, permettant une adaptation continue du modèle aux actions des utilisateurs. Les détails techniques précis sur l'architecture ou les algorithmes sous-jacents ne sont pas explicitement fournis dans le contenu disponible.
deep_analysis.resultats: Les résultats présentés par DeepMind mettent en avant une amélioration significative du réalisme et de la réactivité des simulations générées par Genie 4 par rapport aux générations précédentes. Le modèle serait capable de générer des environnements interactifs avec une cohérence temporelle et spatiale inédite, tout en supportant des interactions complexes. Aucun chiffre clé ou métrique quantitative (comme le taux d'erreur, la latence, ou des comparaisons benchmark) n'est cependant mentionné dans le contenu disponible.
deep_analysis.limites: Le contenu ne permet pas d'identifier clairement les limites de Genie 4, mais on peut supposer que des défis persistent, notamment en termes de généralisation à des environnements non vus lors de l'entraînement, de la consommation computationnelle élevée pour des simulations en temps réel, ou encore de la robustesse face à des interactions imprévues. L'absence de détails sur les données d'entraînement ou les biais potentiels mérite également un regard critique.
deep_analysis.verdict: Genie 4 mérite une attention particulière pour son potentiel à révolutionner la simulation d'environnements virtuels, mais son évaluation technique approfondie nécessitera des publications plus détaillées ou des démonstrations concrètes.

items.title: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals?
items.summary: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ
items.tldr: Ce travail remet en cause l'idée que les tokens discrets visuels perdent nécessairement du sens sémantique, montrant que leur performance dépend davantage du budget de bits effectif que de l'erreur de quantification. Propose FVQ pour améliorer l'efficacité des représentations discrètes, atteignant des performances comparables aux représentations continues.

deep_analysis.probleme: Cette publication remet en question l'hypothèse selon laquelle la quantification des signaux visuels en tokens discrets entraîne nécessairement une perte sémantique irréversible, limitant ainsi leur fidélité par rapport aux représentations visuelles continues. Elle cherche à démontrer que les tokens discrets peuvent rivaliser avec les représentations continues pour des tâches multimodales, malgré les erreurs de quantification traditionnellement perçues comme un obstacle majeur.
deep_analysis.methode: Les auteurs utilisent une approche basée sur la compréhension multimodale comme indicateur de fidélité sémantique. Ils montrent que l'erreur de quantification n'est pas un facteur déterminant, contrairement au budget effectif de bits des indices discrets. Pour surmonter la saturation des quantificateurs existants, ils introduisent la *Factorized Vector Quantization* (FVQ), une méthode qui quantifie des vues complémentaires et fixes des caractéristiques visuelles à l'aide de codebooks parallèles symétriques. Cette technique permet d'améliorer les performances même avec un budget de bits plus élevé. Le modèle est entraîné sur des données multimodales à l'échelle industrielle, avec un objectif de prédiction de tokens partagé entre modalités.
deep_analysis.resultats: Le modèle proposé atteint des performances de pointe parmi les modèles à représentations discrètes, surpassant UniAR et Emu3-Chat de 22,8 % et 59,2 % respectivement, sur une moyenne de neuf métriques. Il est également le premier modèle à représentations discrètes à rivaliser avec des modèles à représentations continues comme Qwen3-VL, y compris sur des tâches fines d'OCR. Les résultats suggèrent que les tokens discrets peuvent égaler les représentations continues en termes de compréhension multimodale.
deep_analysis.limites: Les détails sur la généralisation du modèle à d'autres tâches ou modalités restent limités. De plus, l'évaluation se concentre principalement sur la compréhension multimodale, sans exploration approfondie des impacts sur d'autres aspects comme la génération d'images ou la robustesse aux variations visuelles. Enfin, la dépendance à des données industrielles pourrait poser des questions sur la reproductibilité à plus petite échelle.
deep_analysis.verdict: Cette publication mérite une attention particulière pour son potentiel à redéfinir l'utilisation des tokens discrets dans les modèles multimodaux, offrant une alternative crédible aux représentations continues.

items.title: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
items.summary: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox with no image or video generation model, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, scored by three VLM judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 rank first and second with both the judges and human annotators, and the strongest system satisfies every core requirement on 76.3% of tasks. Delivery is a second axis: counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started, a failure of how agents plan their hour. Agents build their own rendering pipelines and inspect their own frames, yet how much they look does not predict quality. The judges' ranking of the systems closely matches blind human preferences.
items.tldr: VibeVideoBench évalue les agents multimodaux sur la génération vidéo par code, avec un benchmark de 239 tâches et une évaluation hiérarchique rigoureuse. Résultats montrant que les meilleurs systèmes satisfont 76,3% des exigences, avec une corrélation forte entre juges VLM et humains.

deep_analysis.probleme: Les modèles de génération vidéo par diffusion produisent des clips visuellement impressionnants, mais échouent systématiquement à respecter des contraintes précises comme des formules mathématiques exactes, des graphiques corrects, des règles de jeu cohérentes ou une narration synchronisée avec les événements à l'écran. Ce benchmark vise à évaluer des agents multimodaux capables de générer des vidéos via du code, garantissant ainsi une précision et une cohérence technique impossibles à atteindre avec des approches purement génératives.
deep_analysis.methode: VibeVideoBench propose 239 tâches autonomes en anglais et en chinois, couvrant 12 catégories (histoires de données, vidéos musicales, leçons scolaires, explications d'articles scientifiques, etc.). Chaque tâche exige qu'un agent multimodal, exécuté dans son environnement natif et isolé dans un sandbox sans accès à des modèles de génération d'images ou de vidéos, produise un fichier MP4 finalisé avec son en 1 heure maximum. L'évaluation est hiérarchique et basée sur des preuves : vérification du respect des spécifications de livraison via des tests automatisés, application de 13 000 critères spécifiques à chaque tâche (liés aux exigences), et notation sur cinq dimensions de qualité par trois panels de juges (modèles de langage visuel). Les agents doivent construire leurs propres pipelines de rendu et inspecter leurs propres frames, tout en gérant leur temps de calcul.
deep_analysis.resultats: Neuf systèmes d'agents de pointe ont été testés sur 2 151 exécutions évaluées. GPT-6 Astra et Claude Opus 5.5 se classent respectivement premier et deuxième, tant selon les juges automatiques que selon les annotateurs humains. Le meilleur système satisfait toutes les exigences principales dans 76,3 % des tâches. Cependant, la livraison effective des vidéos révèle un deuxième axe de performance : en comptant les vidéos manquantes comme des échecs, le classement change. Trois quarts des vidéos perdues sont dues à des problèmes de planification (rendu commencé trop tard, trop lent, ou jamais lancé). Enfin, la fréquence d'inspection des frames par les agents ne corrèle pas avec la qualité finale.
deep_analysis.limites: Le benchmark repose sur une évaluation automatisée et des juges VLM, dont la fiabilité pour des critères subjectifs (comme la qualité artistique) n'est pas garantie. Les tâches, bien que variées, restent limitées à 239 cas et pourraient ne pas couvrir tous les scénarios réels. De plus, la contrainte d'une heure peut biaiser les résultats en faveur d'agents optimisés pour la rapidité plutôt que pour la robustesse ou la créativité.
deep_analysis.verdict: Ce travail mérite une attention particulière pour son approche innovante combinant génération vidéo par code et évaluation rigoureuse des agents multimodaux, mais ses limites en termes de généralisation et de subjectivité des juges invitent à une interprétation prudente des résultats.

items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
items.summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
items.tldr: PDRVLA introduit un module léger de dynamique physique pour les modèles Vision-Language-Action (VLA), améliorant la génération d'actions robotiques sans latence liée à la prédiction vidéo. Les résultats sur 4 benchmarks montrent des taux de succès élevés (jusqu'à 99,3%), avec des ablations validant l'impact de la supervision par un modèle de monde vidéo et des annotations ECoT.

deep_analysis.probleme: Les modèles Vision-Language-Action (VLA) actuels génèrent des actions robotiques à partir d'observations visuelles et d'instructions en langage naturel, mais leur compréhension des dynamiques physiques des scènes reste superficielle. Cela limite leur capacité à anticiper les conséquences des actions dans des environnements réels, où les interactions physiques sont complexes et continues.
deep_analysis.methode: PDRVLA introduit un *Physical Dynamics Module* léger qui extrait des *tokens physiques* à partir des caractéristiques visuo-linguistiques pour conditionner la génération d'actions, sans nécessiter la génération en ligne de vidéos futures. Ce module est entraîné à prédire directement les caractéristiques futures (RGB, profondeur, flux optique) et bénéficie d'une supervision auxiliaire via un modèle de monde vidéo pré-entraîné et figé. Les données d'entraînement proviennent de sources publiques, enrichies par des techniques comme la synthèse humain-robot, l'annotation de sous-tâches et l'annotation *Embodied Chain-of-Thought* (ECoT). L'architecture évite ainsi la latence induite par la génération de vidéos tout en intégrant une représentation explicite des dynamiques physiques.
deep_analysis.resultats: PDRVLA atteint des taux de succès élevés sur quatre benchmarks de simulation : 99,3 % sur LIBERO, 89,9 % sur LIBERO-Plus, 93,6 % sur RoboTwin 2.0, et 81,5 % sur SimplerEnv. Les ablations démontrent que la supervision par un modèle de monde améliore la prédiction des états futurs, et que des techniques comme le conditionnement par sous-tâches ou l'ECoT influencent positivement les performances. Les résultats suggèrent une meilleure généralisation grâce à l'intégration des dynamiques physiques.
deep_analysis.limites: Le contenu disponible ne précise pas les performances en conditions réelles (hors simulation), ni les coûts computationnels exacts du module de dynamique physique. L'efficacité de l'approche dépend fortement de la qualité des données synthétiques et des annotations ECoT, dont la scalabilité n'est pas démontrée. Enfin, l'absence de détails sur les architectures sous-jacentes (ex. : modèle de monde vidéo utilisé) limite l'évaluation de la robustesse.
deep_analysis.verdict: Ce travail mérite une attention particulière pour son approche innovante combinant représentation des dynamiques physiques et efficacité computationnelle, mais son applicabilité réelle et sa scalabilité restent à valider.

items.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
items.tldr: Propose une méthode pour optimiser l'inférence des modèles Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) en évitant le besoin de données de calibration pour la sélection des canaux. Utilise une approche top-k pour réduire la mémoire et les calculs sans perte de performance, tout en évitant des problèmes comme la répétition dans les réponses.

items.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
items.summary: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
items.tldr: Analyse systématique de l'utilité des systèmes de mémoire pour les agents, montrant que beaucoup sous-performent le RAG naïf. Introduit les concepts de 'memory benefit' et 'memory tax' pour évaluer l'impact net des mécanismes de mémoire sur les performances.

items.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
items.tldr: Propose ThinkWorld, un cadre pour les modèles VLA (Vision-Language-Action) combinant raisonnement en chaîne de dynamique (CoD) et apprentissage par renforcement avec imagination du monde. Permet d'exploiter des vidéos non annotées pour améliorer la généralisation des actions robotiques.

items.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
items.summary: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
items.tldr: Introduit Omni-InteractScope, un benchmark de 1 479 interactions annotées pour évaluer la capacité des Omni-LLMs à interagir de manière proactive dans des flux audiovisuels continus. Révèle des limites critiques dans l'invocation d'outils et les rappels sans requête.

items.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
items.summary: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
items.tldr: Propose HABIT-Bench, un benchmark pour évaluer l'induction d'habitudes à partir d'événements faibles dans la mémoire des agents. Montre que les méthodes actuelles peinent à inférer et appliquer correctement les habitudes, même avec des données annotées.

items.title: Multiscale Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents interact with their environments through complete assistant turns while generating each action token by token. We observe that critic values vary primarily across turns, motivating optimization anchored at turns with finer credit allocation among tokens. We propose Multiscale Policy Optimization (MPO), combining Multiscale Advantage Estimation (MAE) and turn-level importance sampling to align credit assignment and policy updates at the turn scale. Extensive experiments across search, tool-use, and automation tasks with 4B and 30B-A3B models demonstrate consistent gains over strong RL baselines.
items.tldr: MPO améliore l'optimisation des agents LLM à long terme en allouant des crédits à l'échelle des tours plutôt qu'à l'échelle des tokens, avec des gains démontrés sur des tâches de recherche, d'usage d'outils et d'automatisation. Approche solide et applicable, avec des résultats expérimentaux robustes.

items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
items.summary: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.
items.tldr: The Trinity propose un cadre de *self-improvement* récursif pour agents multimodaux, combinant génération de mondes et évolution de *harnesses* via trois rôles (Créateur, Explorateur, Évolueur). Le système réorganise les tâches en un arbre de capacités hiérarchiques, permettant une adaptation scalable à la complexité des tâches.

items.title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
items.summary: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. Project Page: https://y0uroy.github.io/JAM
items.tldr: JAM unifie les approches VLA et WAM en proposant un modèle 'Just Action' avec une perte de prédiction future (sans génération visuelle) et une perte d'action. Les résultats montrent que cette architecture dépasse les variantes FastWAM et ImageWAM sur LIBERO, clarifiant les débats sur les backbones et objectifs.

items.title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning
items.summary: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
items.tldr: Démonstration théorique et empirique de l'existence d'un 'écart structurel' : les modèles sans connaissance explicite de la structure sous-jacente d'un problème (ex: solveur, symétries) nécessitent des données infinies pour égaler les performances d'un modèle structuré, même asymptotiquement.

items.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
items.summary: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

extra.authors: Saket Reddy, Amro Abbas, Anshuman Suri, Ari Morcos, David Schwab, Pratyush Maini

items.tldr: Méthode *SimpleLoRIF* pour identifier les données de fine-tuning dégradant la sécurité des LLM via des gradients, permettant de filtrer 20% des exemples les plus dangereux et réduisant les attaques GCG de 22%. Outil pratique pour l'optimisation sécurisée des modèles.

items.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
items.summary: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.
items.tldr: h1 démontre qu'un agent simple avec interface Lean 4 et réflexion autonome atteint des performances de pointe en preuve formelle, égalant des workflows spécialisés sans complexité additionnelle. Résultat surprenant qui questionne les architectures sur-mesure en raisonnement formel.

items.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
items.summary: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
items.tldr: Étude systématique sur l'entraînement des transformers bouclés avec BPTT tronqué, démontrant que la rétropropagation complète est plus efficace en termes de calcul pour des performances optimales. Fournit une loi de scaling unifiée pour guider les choix d'architecture et d'entraînement.

items.title: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?
items.summary: Video captioning aims to preserve visual information through compact descriptions, predominantly using natural language. However, precisely expressing fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics in natural language often leads to lengthy and potentially ambiguous descriptions. In this work, we explore Code as Video Caption, a paradigm where executable programs serve as a complementary representation of visual content through graphical primitives, layout rules, and functions of time. To examine whether code captions effectively preserve video information, we compare them with natural language captions on downstream question answering and video reconstruction tasks. Our results show that code captions achieve superior reasoning accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Despite these advantages, realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate faithful code captions. To systematically assess this capability, we introduce CodeCap-Bench, which comprises 323 videos spanning five categories of structured 2D content, along with fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework. Extensive experiments reveal that while leading proprietary MLLMs demonstrate promising code captioning capabilities, they still struggle to faithfully capture complex temporal dynamics, with open-source models lagging substantially behind.
items.tldr: Explore l'utilisation de code comme représentation alternative aux légendes textuelles pour les vidéos, améliorant la précision des tâches de QA et de reconstruction. Introduit CodeCap-Bench pour évaluer la capacité des MLLMs à générer des légendes en code de manière fidèle.

items.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
items.summary: Recent test-time training (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient test-time adaptation method for scientific discovery. We introduce Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by 82.8-84.6% in FLOPs and 47.7-58.4% in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
items.tldr: Introduit Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), une méthode d'adaptation en temps réel pour les LLMs en tâches de découverte scientifique. Surpasse le Test-Time Training (TTT) en performance tout en réduisant les coûts de calcul de 47-84% en FLOPs et temps d'exécution.

items.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
items.summary: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.
items.tldr: Analyse économique des réglages d'effort de raisonnement des LLM, montrant que l'augmentation de l'effort ne garantit pas de meilleurs résultats et peut être coûteuse (jusqu'à 42x plus cher). Essentiel pour comprendre le *trade-off* coût-performance des agents.

items.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
items.summary: Education Innovation
items.tldr: Le framework SLEEP (Google Research) propose une méthode pour que les LLM conservent des connaissances en apprentissage continu, via un mécanisme de 'sommeil'. Approche prometteuse pour l'adaptabilité des modèles, avec des fondations théoriques solides.

items.title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
items.summary: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

extra.authors: Andrew Szot, Samira Abnar, Omar Attia, Abbas Kazerouni, Michael Kirchhof, Cheng-Yu Hsieh

items.tldr: Scaling laws pour les agents utilisant des outils, dérivées de 458k tâches synthétiques, montrant que la diversité des outils et bases de données est plus critique que le volume de tâches. Guide pratique pour l'entraînement d'agents performants et généralisables.

items.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
items.summary: Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state. MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys. Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks. In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory. MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.

extra.authors: Hee Seung Hwang, Sanghyuk Chun, Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky, Zhiwei Deng

items.tldr: MERLIN introduit une attention linéaire multi-états (MSLA) améliorée par une agrégation basée sur les moments (moyenne et variance) des clés segmentées, permettant une modélisation plus fine de la pertinence des segments pour les requêtes. Les résultats montrent des gains consistants sur des tâches de long contexte (Gated DeltaNet-1.3B, Mamba-2-780M), avec une complexité linéaire.

items.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
items.summary: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.
items.tldr: Cet article propose une évaluation critique des *world models* latents, introduisant le concept de *faithful latent world models* et la métrique *Latent Rollout Consistency (LRC)* pour mesurer leur capacité à capturer la dynamique sous-jacente de l'environnement. Les résultats montrent que les modèles SOTA échouent à modéliser fidèlement les transitions environnementales, soulignant un gap entre performance et compréhension structurelle.

items.title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
items.summary: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.

extra.authors: Baptiste Bonin, Caro Strickland, Audrey Durand

items.tldr: Méthode d'évaluation (CRS) pour la manipulation d'objets articulés, distinguant la progression utile le long des axes de mouvement de la rotation inefficace hors contrainte. Validation sur 74 objets simulés et démonstration de transferts de compétences entre portes et tiroirs, avec une robustesse aux erreurs d'axe jusqu'à 30°.

items.title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
items.summary: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.

extra.authors: Anukriti Singh, Maxime Caniot, Pratap Tokekar, Firas Abi-Farraj

items.tldr: Module léger (ARC) pour corriger les échecs localisés de politiques de manipulation robotique via des corrections humaines éparses et du RL. Améliore le taux de succès de 33.3% à 75% sur des tâches réelles, en exploitant des sous-espaces de correction 2-3D dans l'espace d'action résiduel.

items.title: From Interaction to Capability: Task Advancement as State and Supervision for GUI Agents
items.summary: GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.

extra.authors: Ziyang Chen, Qian Li, Chengwei Qin

items.tldr: Nouvelle architecture mémoire (*Task Advancement Memory*) pour agents GUI, améliorant la réutilisation des opérations et la réussite des tâches multi-applications via un suivi des progrès vérifiés. Avancée majeure pour les agents autonomes en interfaces graphiques.

items.title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
items.summary: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.
items.tldr: Bibliothèque Concordat implémente des protocoles typés (session types) pour contraindre dynamiquement les actions d'agents LLM, éliminant les effets de bord indésirables et améliorant la fiabilité sur des tâches critiques comme la gestion de réservations aériennes.

items.title: CRISP: Co-designing Pruning and Scheduling for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge Servers
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained edge platforms is often dominated by expert-weight movement rather than computation. Although each token activates only a small subset of experts, routing is input-dependent, so all experts must remain accessible and memory movement dominates latency. Existing approaches such as uniform pruning and expert dropping overlook two properties of MoE execution: expert combinations are highly skewed in frequency, and experts contribute asymmetrically within each combination. We present CRISP, a combination-aware framework that co-designs pruning and runtime scheduling for efficient MoE serving on memory-constrained edge platforms. CRISP reorders neurons by importance so one stored expert can support multiple execution widths, assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations based on frequency and expert role, and exploits heterogeneous widths to overlap expert loading with computation. Across Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, CRISP improves throughput by up to $2.1\times$ at the same memory budget while limiting accuracy loss to 3.6\% relative to full-width inference. Our results highlight that efficient edge MoE serving requires jointly optimizing which expert capacity is preserved and how expert execution is scheduled.

extra.authors: Congwei Zhang, Youming Tao, Yifei Zou, Yu Yang, Ruirui Zhang, Xiaoyu Zhang

items.tldr: CRISP co-conçoit élagage et ordonnancement pour l'inférence MoE sur serveurs edge, exploitant la fréquence asymétrique des combinaisons d'experts et leur rôle différencié pour améliorer le débit jusqu'à 2.1× avec une perte d'exactitude limitée à 3.6%.

items.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
items.summary: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.
items.tldr: Étude sur la mémoire des groupes LLM montrant que les heuristiques de sélection (rareté ou pertinence) échouent à capturer l'information utile pour les décisions, avec des biais systématiques comme l'effet de preuve sociale. Analyse rigoureuse avec un benchmark CrossProfile et implications pour les systèmes multi-agents.

items.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
items.summary: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
items.tldr: EvidenceConnect génère des données synthétiques pour améliorer la perception multimodale en connectant des preuves visuelles via des zooms ciblés, formant des questions nécessitant agrégation ou enchaînement d'informations. Approche innovante pour renforcer les capacités de raisonnement visuel sans données coûteuses.
